韩语语序和中文不一样.en: Korean word order differs from Chinese

只需要记住一件事，就能看懂大多数韩语句子。\\n和中文最大的不同：\\n动词永远.en: Just remember one thing, and you'll understand most Korean sentences.\nThe biggest difference from Chinese:\nThe verb always comes at the end of the sentence, while in Chinese the verb is in the middle.

下面展示的是韩语最基本的句子框架。\\n不需要背，先看懂每个位置放什么就够了。.en: Below is the most basic Korean sentence framework.\nNo need to memorize it—just understand what goes in each position.

韩语靠\"助词\"标记每个词的角色，所以词序比中文灵活。\\n这几条规则是骨架，.en: Korean uses "particles" to mark each word's role, so word order is more flexible than in Chinese.\nThese rules are the backbone, and every lesson from here on will use them.

韩语的SOV语序在所有场合都适用从日常聊天到正式演讲。\\n先记住动词永远在句末.en: Korean's SOV word order applies in all situations, from everyday chats to formal speeches.\nFirst, remember that the verb always comes at the end—everything else will come with time.

先看句尾，再往前拆.en: Look at the Ending First, Then Break It Down

一种语气，搞定面试、课堂、公告三大场景。.en: One tone that covers three scenarios: interviews, classrooms, and announcements.

下面是正式体的三种句型。\\n先认识「词干有无收音→词尾变化」这一条，剩下的靠感.en: Below are the three sentence types in the formal style.\nFirst, learn the rule "whether the stem ends with a consonant or vowel → ending changes," and the rest will stick naturally.

词尾变化只看一件事：\\n词干最后一个音节有没有收音（받침）。\\n这和中文完全.en: The ending change depends on only one thing: \nwhether the last syllable of the stem has a final consonant (받침). \nThis is completely different from Chinese, but two rules cover all cases.

正式体用在面试、课堂提问、公开演讲、新闻播报。\\n和朋友或平辈说话用这种语气会.en: The formal style is used in interviews, classroom questions, public speeches, and news broadcasts. \nUsing this tone with friends or peers sounds stiff; for everyday conversation, you'll learn that in the next lesson.

日常对话最常用的说法.en: The most common expression in everyday conversation

和朋友聊天、发动态、追剧评论，全靠这一课。\\n和中文不同：\\n韩语动词分两套.en: Chatting with friends, posting updates, commenting on shows—all rely on this lesson. \nUnlike Chinese: \nKorean verbs have two sets of forms. 하다 verbs directly become 해요, while other verbs depend on the last vowel of the stem to decide whether to attach 아요 or 어요.

这节课的句型是日常生活里用得最多的。\\n同样先看框架，不用担心所有变化规则，练.en: The sentence patterns in this lesson are the most used in daily life. \nAgain, look at the framework first—don't worry about all the change rules; you'll naturally remember them through practice.

变化规则看起来多，但核心只有一条：\\n词干最后的元音决定用 아요 还是 어요。.en: The change rules may seem like many, but the core is just one: \nthe last vowel of the stem determines whether to use 아요 or 어요. \nFor 하다 verbs, just memorize 해요.

해요 体是韩语里使用频率最高的语体，聊天、发消息、追剧评论、和陌生人对话都用这个.en: The 해요 style is the most frequently used speech level in Korean—used in chatting, texting, commenting on shows, and talking to strangers. \nMaster this lesson, and you can handle 80% of everyday situations.

一个助词，让对方知道你接下来要说谁/什么，还能制造对比感。.en: A particle that lets the listener know who or what you're about to talk about, and can also create a sense of contrast.

은/는 加在句子主题后面，告诉听者「接下来说的是关于这个的」。\\n下面的结构展.en: 은/는 is attached after the topic of the sentence, telling the listener "what follows is about this."\nThe structure below shows where it appears.

只需要看一件事：\\n这个词最后有没有收音（받침）。\\n有收音用 은，没有用.en:
You only need to check one thing:
Does the word end with a final consonant (받침)?
If it has a final consonant, use 은; if not, use 는.
This rule applies to all Korean particles, so mastering it is very useful.

은/는 在几乎所有句子里都会出现自我介绍、描述事物、做对比都用它。\\n中文通常.en: 은/는 appears in almost every sentence—introducing yourself, describing things, and making comparisons all use it.\nIn Chinese, this position is often omitted, so beginners tend to forget to add it.

标出动作的对象.en: Marks the object of an action

을/를 标记动作的对象，也就是宾语。韩语靠을/를标出宾语，相当于告诉听者「动作落.en: 을/를 marks the object of an action, i.e., the direct object. Korean uses 을/를 to indicate the object, essentially telling the listener "who the action falls on"—it must be added every time and cannot be omitted.

을/를 标记「动作的对象是谁」，位置在动词前面。\\n下面的结构展示它在句子里的.en: 을/를 marks "who the action's object is," and it appears before the verb.\nThe structure below shows its position in the sentence.

跟 은/는 一样，只看最后有没有收音（받침）。\\n有收音用 을，没有用 를。\.en: Same as 은/는, just check if there's a final consonant (받침).\nUse 을 if there's a final consonant, 를 if there isn't.\nTwo rules, remember in a minute.

只要句子里有动作（吃、喝、看、学……），动作对象后面就要加 을/를。\\n中文不.en: As long as there's an action in the sentence (eat, drink, see, study...), add 을/를 after the object of the action.\nChinese doesn't need this marker, so you'll often forget to add it at first.

에 可以表示去哪里、在哪里、几点，意思取决于后面的动词。\\n和中文不同：\\n.en: 에 can indicate going somewhere, being somewhere, or a specific time—the meaning depends on the verb that follows.\nUnlike Chinese: \nChinese uses three separate words "在/去/到", but Korean uses 에 uniformly, distinguishing the meaning through the accompanying verb.

에 有三种用法，但形式完全一样。\\n下面展示三种句型，靠后面的动词就能判断是哪.en: 에 has three uses, but the form is exactly the same.\nBelow are three sentence patterns—the verb that follows tells you which use it is.

에 的规则简单：\\n直接加在时间词或地点词后面，不看收音。\\n关键是后面配什.en:
The rule for 에 is simple: 
Just attach it directly after a time or place word, regardless of final consonants.
The key is what verb follows: 
가다/오다→direction, 있다/없다→existence, time+에→point in time.

에 在日常对话里极其常见说去哪里、在哪里、几点都用它。\\n中文的\"在/去/到.en: 에 is extremely common in everyday conversation—use it for going somewhere, being somewhere, or what time.\nChinese uses three words "在/去/到", but Korean uses 에 uniformly, distinguishing meaning through the verb.

判断对错：에 的用法.en: True or False: Uses of 에

动作 + 地点的专属搭档，只要是\"真的在做什么\"就用 에서。\\n和中文不同.en: Action + location's exclusive partner — use 에서 whenever you're "actually doing something."\nUnlike Chinese:\nIn Chinese, "在" covers both "being at" and "doing at" a place, but Korean distinguishes between 에 (existence/direction) and 에서 (where an action takes place).

에서 只有一个用法：\\n在哪里「做」动作。\\n下面的结构展示它和动词的搭配方.en: 에서 has only one use:\nWhere you "do" an action.\nThe structure below shows how it pairs with verbs.

判断用 에 还是 에서 只需要问一句话：\\n这里是「真的在做某件事」，还是「只.en: To decide between 에 and 에서, ask just one question:\nAre you "actually doing something" here, or just "existing/being there"? Doing something → 에서, existing/going → 에.

几乎所有「在某地做某事」的句子都需要 에서在咖啡店工作、在学校学习、在家休息。\.en: Almost every sentence about "doing something somewhere" needs 에서 — working at a café, studying at school, resting at home.\nDistinguishing it from 에 is the most important P1 distinction, worth extra practice.

에서 vs 에 — 一张表搞清楚.en: 에서 vs 에 — One Table to Clear It Up

说过去做了什么.en: Saying what you did in the past

词干末元音决定用哪个词尾，三条规则搞定所有过去时。\\n和中文「了」不同的是：\.en: The final vowel of the stem determines which ending to use — three rules cover all past tense forms.\nUnlike Chinese "了":\nKorean past tense simply means "already happened," not a change of state or a continuing result.

过去时只改动词/形容词的词尾，主语和助词完全不变。\\n下面展示变化后的句型框架.en: The past tense only changes the verb/adjective ending; the subject and particles stay exactly the same.\nBelow is the sentence frame after the change.

过去时词尾由词干最后的元音决定：\\nㅏ/ㅗ 结尾→ 았어요，其他元音→ 었어요.en: The past tense ending is determined by the final vowel of the stem:\nEnds in ㅏ/ㅗ → 았어요, other vowels → 었어요, 하다 → 했어요.\nThese three rules cover 99% of words.

写日记、讲昨天发生的事、追剧聊剧情都需要过去时。\\n和中文的「了」不完全一样韩.en: Writing a diary, talking about yesterday, or discussing a drama plot all require the past tense.\nIt's not exactly the same as Chinese "了" — Korean past tense simply marks "already happened," unlike Chinese "了," which can also indicate a change or a continuing result.

说将来打算做什么.en: Talk about what you plan to do in the future

-을/ㄹ 거예요 表示要做/会做/打算做，两条规则搞定。\\n和中文不同：\\n.en: -을/ㄹ 거예요 expresses doing, will do, or planning to do—just two rules to master.\nUnlike Chinese: In Chinese, "要/会/打算" are separate words, but Korean expresses all three meanings with a single ending attached to the verb.

将来时在现在时的基础上只改动词词尾，结构位置完全相同。\\n下面展示变化后的句型.en: The future tense only changes the verb ending based on the present tense; the sentence structure stays exactly the same.\nBelow shows the transformed sentence patterns.

将来时只看一件事：\\n词干最后有没有收音。\\n有收音加을 거예요，没有收音加.en: For the future tense, only one thing matters: whether the verb stem ends with a final consonant (받침).\nIf it has a final consonant, add 을 거예요; if not, add ㄹ 거예요.\nIt's simpler than the past tense—only two rules.

说计划、约定、推测都用-을/ㄹ 거예요。\\n它同时覆盖中文的「要/会/打算」三.en: Use -을/ㄹ 거예요 for plans, promises, and predictions.\nIt covers all three Chinese meanings of "要/会/打算" in one ending—three uses, one form.

说正在做什么.en: Talk about what is happening right now

动词词干 + 고 있어요，比过去时和将来时都简单，不用判断元音。\\n和中文不同.en: Verb stem + 고 있어요. It's simpler than past and future tenses—no need to check vowels.\nUnlike Chinese: Chinese expresses ongoing actions with "正在/着," while Korean embeds the progressive meaning directly into the verb ending, without adding extra words.

进行时只有一套公式：\\n动词词干 + 고 있어요。\\n不用判断元音、不用看收.en:
The progressive tense has only one formula:
Verb stem + 고 있어요.
No vowel checks, no batchim rules—it's the easiest grammar in Chapter 1.
The key is understanding the difference between "doing right now" and "habitual action."

最大陷阱：\\n하다 动词接고时保持原形，공부하고 있어요 而不是 공부해고 있.en: Biggest trap: When 하다 verbs take 고, keep the original form—공부하고 있어요, not 공부해고 있어요.\nAlso, adjectives (좋다, 예쁘다) describe states, not actions, so they can't take -고 있어요.

对方问\"你在干嘛？\"时，如果是此刻正在做的事就用进行时；\\n如果是表达习惯.en: When someone asks "What are you doing?" use the progressive tense if it's something happening right now;\nuse the plain present tense for habits or identity.\nThe progressive appears very often in daily situations like texting, binge-watching shows, or waiting for someone.

判断对错：-고 있어요 进行时.en: True or False: -고 있어요 Progressive Tense

完成这份练习，检验前 10 课是否掌握。\\n10 题，5 阶段循序渐进：识别.en: Complete this practice to check if you've mastered the first 10 lessons.\n10 questions, 5 progressive stages: Identify 2 → Transform 3 → Choose 2 → Correct 2 → Apply 1.

第一章10节课的核心主线：\\n韩语语序（SOV）、两种礼貌体、六个助词（은/는.en: The core thread of Chapter 1's 10 lessons:\nKorean word order (SOV), two polite speech levels, six particles (은/는/을/를/에/에서), and three tenses (past/future/progressive).\nThis practice covers all the key points—finish it to see what you haven't mastered yet.

说去哪里、和谁一起.en: Saying where you're going and who you're with

两个核心：\\n说目的地用 에 가요，说\"和……一起\"用 와/과 或 하고。.en:
Two key points:
Use 에 가요 to say where you're going, and 와/과 or 하고 to say "with whom."
In Chinese, "go" and "with" are two separate words, but in Korean, particles are attached directly to nouns—no separate verb needed.

这节课有两个句型：\\n去哪里（에 가요）、和谁一起（와/과/하고）。\\n先看.en:
This lesson has two sentence patterns:
Where to go (에 가요) and with whom (와/과/하고).
First, see clearly where each one sits in the sentence.

와/과 的选择只看一件事：\\n前面名词最后有没有收音。\\n口语直接用하고，不.en:
Choosing between 와 and 과 depends on just one thing:
whether the noun before it ends with a final consonant (받침).
In speech, you can just use 하고 without worrying about the final consonant—it's easier and more natural.

约朋友、出行、购物是用这套语法最频繁的场景约朋友去哪里、买东西\"和\"什么都用.en: Making plans with friends, going out, and shopping are the most common situations for this grammar. Asking where to meet, what to buy "with" whom—you'll use it all the time.

说有没有、人在不在.en: Say whether something exists or someone is present

있어요 表示\"有\"或\"在\"，없어요 表示\"没有\"或\"不在\"，主语.en:
있어요 means "there is" or "is here," and 없어요 means "there isn't" or "isn't here." The subject is marked with 이/가.
Unlike Chinese, Korean uses the same sentence pattern for "I have a book" and "The book is here"—the only difference is whether you mention the location.

这节课有三种句型：\\n说\"有/没有\"、说\"在哪里\"、说\"某地有什么\.en:
This lesson has three sentence patterns:
Saying "have/don't have," saying "where something is," and saying "what is in a place."
All three revolve around 있어요/없어요. First, check whether the location word is in the sentence.

이/가 的选择只看主语名词最后一个字有没有收音。\\n有收音接 이，没有收音接.en:
Choosing between 이 and 가 depends only on whether the last syllable of the subject noun has a final consonant (받침).
With a final consonant, use 이; without one, use 가.
This follows the same logic as 은/는 from P1, just with a different particle function.

있어요/없어요 在日常对话里出现频率极高找东西、约时间、描述房间、拒绝邀请，全都.en:
있어요/없어요 appear constantly in everyday conversation—looking for things, making plans, describing a room, turning down an invitation—you'll use them everywhere.
Master this lesson and you'll cover 80% of the "have/have not" situations in daily Korean.

邀请别人一起做，或礼貌请求.en: Invite others to do something together, or make a polite request

-ㅂ시다/읍시다 是\"我们一起……吧\"，-(으)세요 是礼貌地请对方做某事。.en: -ㅂ시다/읍시다 means "let's ... together," while -(으)세요 is a polite way to ask someone to do something.\nComparing to Chinese: \nㅂ시다 ≈ "let's ..." (the speaker participates too), 세요 ≈ "please ..." (only asking the other person to do it).

这节课有两套词尾：\\nㅂ시다/읍시다 用来发出邀请，(으)세요 用来礼貌请求。.en: This lesson has two sets of endings: \nㅂ시다/읍시다 is used for invitations, and (으)세요 is used for polite requests. \nBoth sets require conjugation, so first figure out which situation calls for which set.

变形规则和之前一样，只看词干最后有没有收音：\\n无收音接 -ㅂ시다/-세요，有.en:
The conjugation rules are the same as before—just look at whether the stem ends in a final consonant: 
No final consonant → attach -ㅂ시다/-세요; final consonant → attach -읍시다/-으세요. 
The exception is stems ending in ㄹ: 
The ㄹ drops and -ㅂ시다 is attached (알다→압시다).

세요 在餐厅、课堂、服务业随处可见\"请坐\"\"请看\"；\\nㅂ시다 则是约.en: 세요 is everywhere in restaurants, classrooms, and service settings—"please sit," "please look." \nㅂ시다 is for inviting friends—"let's go together," "let's study together." \nThese two endings will instantly make your Korean sound more polite.

数东西、点餐、报人数.en: Counting things, ordering food, stating the number of people

韩语数字有两套：\\n固有数词（하나/둘…）配个/人/杯，汉字数词（일/이/삼….en: Korean has two number systems: \nNative numbers (하나/둘…) are used with counters for items/people/cups, while Sino-Korean numbers (일/이/삼…) are used for money/dates/phone numbers. \nChinese has only one number system; Korean has two because Sino-Korean numbers were borrowed historically, while native numbers were kept for counting physical objects.

这节课核心是\"数字 + 量词\"的搭配。\\n先认识两套数字各自负责什么，再看.en: The core of this lesson is the combination of "number + counter."\nFirst, learn what each of the two number systems is responsible for, then look at the pattern of where the counter goes after the number.

搞清楚两件事：①固有数词 vs 汉字数词数实物用固有（개/명/잔），数钱/时间分.en: Understand two things: ① Native Korean numbers vs. Sino-Korean numbers—use native numbers for counting objects (개/명/잔), and Sino-Korean numbers for money/time minutes/dates.\n② Native numbers shorten before counters:\n하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, the rest stay the same.

点餐、购物、订位是用数词最集中的场景。\\n掌握\"커피 한 잔 주세요\"这一.en: Ordering food, shopping, and making reservations are the most common situations for using numbers.\nMaster the pattern "커피 한 잔 주세요" and you'll get by smoothly at coffee shops, restaurants, and convenience stores.

三个小助词各有一招：\\n의 标所属，도 加\"也\"，만 限制\"只有\"。\.en: Three small particles each have their own role:\n의 marks possession, 도 adds "also," and 만 limits to "only."\nAll three attach after nouns, but their functions are completely different—similar to Chinese "的/也/只," once you recognize the function, the usage becomes clear.

这节课三个助词各自独立，不需要接续变形。\\n重点是搞清楚每个助词替换掉的是哪个.en: In this lesson, the three particles are independent and don't require conjugation changes.\nThe key is understanding which position each particle replaces:\n도 and 만 replace 은/는/이/가/을/를.

의 在口语里常省略（내 친구 比 나의 친구 更自然）；\\n도 和 만 会吃掉.en: 의 is often omitted in spoken language (내 친구 sounds more natural than 나의 친구);\n도 and 만 absorb the preceding case particle (은/는/이/가/을/를) and cannot stack on the same noun (커피도만 ✗).

도 在日常对话里频率极高\"我也是\"\"我也想去\"，每次附和都用得到；\\n.en: 도 appears extremely frequently in daily conversation—"me too," "I also want to go"—you'll use it every time you agree;\n만 is used to emphasize "just this/only this," handy for ordering, confessing, or setting limits.

안 是最简单的否定，-지 않다 更完整；\\n그리고 连接补充信息，그렇지만 连.en: 안 is the simplest negation, -지 않다 is more complete; 그리고 connects additional information, 그렇지만 connects contrast. This lesson combines "negation" and "conjunctions" because once you can make negative sentences, you need conjunctions to combine information. In Chinese, "not go" simply puts "不" before the verb; in Korean, 안 goes in the same position, but 하다 verbs must be split: 공부 안 해요 (not 안 공부해요).

这节课分两块：\\n否定（안 / -지 않다）和连词（그리고 / 그렇지만）。\.en: This lesson has two parts: negation (안 / -지 않다) and conjunctions (그리고 / 그렇지만). First get the two ways of negating clear, then see how conjunctions link two sentences together.

否定有两条路：\\n안 直接放动词前（口语快速否定）；\\n-지 않아요 接词干.en: There are two ways to negate: 안 goes directly before the verb (quick spoken negation); -지 않아요 attaches to the stem (more complete and more written). 하다 verbs are special—you say 공부 안 해요, not 안 공부해요.

能说\"不\"是日常对话的基础拒绝邀请、说饮食偏好、表达不喜欢，全靠否定句。\\.en: Being able to say "no" is essential for daily conversation—declining invitations, stating food preferences, and expressing dislikes all rely on negative sentences. Adding 그렇지만 (but) lets you express "although... but..." contrast, making your speech more natural.

选择正确的否定或连接词.en: Choose the correct negation or conjunction

指出\"这个/那个\"，标出主语.en: Point out "this/that" and mark the subject

이/가 标记主语或引入新信息；\\n이・그・저 是指示词，放名词前表示\"这个/.en: 이/가 marks the subject or introduces new information; 이・그・저 are demonstratives placed before nouns to mean "this/that/that over there." Note: 이/가 is the subject particle you learned in P1—this lesson focuses on combining it with demonstratives and understanding its "introducing new information" function. In Chinese, "this/that" doesn't distinguish three distances, but Korean's 이/그/저 strictly separates three distances: near the speaker, near the listener, and far from both.

这节课两块内容：\\n이/가 的进阶用法（强调和引入新信息）+ 指示词이/그/저.en: This lesson has two parts: advanced uses of 이/가 (emphasis and introducing new information) + the demonstratives 이/그/저. Demonstratives go before nouns, while 이/가 goes after nouns—different positions, different functions.

이/그/저 按距离区分：\\n이=说话人附近，그=听话人附近或刚提到的事物，저=.en: 이/그/저 are distinguished by distance: 이 = near the speaker, 그 = near the listener or something just mentioned, 저 = far from both. In speech, 이것/그것/저것 contract to 이거/그거/저거. The final-consonant rules for 이/가 are exactly the same as in P1.

指示词是购物、聊K-pop、看剧时最常用的表达\"这首歌\"\"那个演员\"\".en: Demonstratives are the most common expressions when shopping, chatting about K-pop, or watching dramas—like "this song," "that actor," or "how much is this?" After this lesson, you'll be able to point at someone or something more precisely.

选择正确的助词或指示词.en: Choose the Correct Particle or Demonstrative

说从几点到几点、从哪到哪.en: Saying from what time to what time, from where to where

부터 表示起点\"从\"，까지 表示终点\"到\"，时间说法：\\n시간은 固有.en: 부터 marks the starting point "from", and 까지 marks the endpoint "to". For telling time: hours use native Korean numbers, minutes use Sino-Korean numbers.\nThis lesson applies the numbers learned in P2-L04 directly to time expressions, while also learning the range pattern "from...to...".\nThe Chinese structure "from three to five o'clock" is the same as Korean, but Korean uses native numbers for "hours" and Sino-Korean numbers for "minutes"—mixing the two systems is a challenge that doesn't exist in Chinese.

两个核心词 부터/까지 结构很简单：\\n直接贴在时间/地点词后面。\\n难点在.en: The structure with the two core words 부터/까지 is simple: they attach directly after time/place words.\nThe tricky part is reading time—hours use native numbers, minutes use Sino-Korean numbers, mixing both systems.

时间读法只需记住：\\n시（点）用固有数词（한/두/세…열두），분（分）用汉字数.en: For reading time, just remember: 시 (hour) uses native numbers (한/두/세…열두), 분 (minute) uses Sino-Korean numbers (일/이/십…오십오).\nSpecial cases: half-hour is 반 (두 시 반 = 2:30).\nFor spatial starting points use 에서, for temporal starting points use 부터—they cannot be mixed.

说工作时间、约定见面、描述演唱会时间，부터/까지 是最常用的时间表达框架。\\n.en: When talking about work hours, making plans to meet, or describing concert times, 부터/까지 is the most common time expression framework.\nMaster this lesson and you can accurately state any "from X to X" arrangement.

说\"给谁/对谁\"，认识词尾变形.en: Learn how to say "to whom" and recognize irregular verb endings

에게/한테 表示动作的对象（给谁/对谁）；\\nㅂ 不规则：\\n덥다→더워요，.en:
에게/한테 indicates the recipient of an action (to whom/for whom);
ㅂ irregular: 덥다→더워요, some words ending in ㅂ change to 워요 when followed by a vowel.
These two points may seem unrelated, but both are about "actions with a recipient"—using 에게/한테 for people, and irregular weather adjectives to describe your surroundings.
In Chinese, "to a friend" has only one form, but Korean distinguishes by speech level: 에게 (written) and 한테 (spoken), a distinction that doesn't exist in Chinese.

两块内容：①에게/한테（给谁/对谁）接在人名或人称词后面；\\n②ㅂ 不规则变形.en: Two parts: ①에게/한테 (to whom/for whom) attaches to names or person nouns;\n②The ㅂ irregular only affects weather/feeling adjectives.\nUnderstand each part separately first, then combine them.

에게 是书面/正式，한테 是口语。\\n收/发方向区别：\\n送出去用 에게/한.en:
에게 is written/formal, 한테 is spoken.
Direction difference:
Use 에게/한테 when sending out, and 에게서/한테서 when receiving from someone.
ㅂ irregular:
Check if the stem ends in ㅂ; when followed by a vowel, ㅂ changes to 워.
Note: 입다 (to wear) and 잡다 (to catch) are regular and do not change.

한테 是韩语聊天里最常见的词之一\"给朋友发消息\"\"从朋友那里收到礼物\"都.en: 한테 is one of the most common words in Korean texting—"send a message to a friend" and "receive a gift from a friend" both use it.\nWeather words (더워요/추워요) are expressions you might use every day, so you can start using them in your diary and conversations right away.

ㅂ 不规则常用词速记.en: Quick Memorization of Common ㅂ Irregular Words

认识两类常见不规则变形.en: Learn two common types of irregular conjugations

两类变形规则：\\nㄷ 不规则（部分 ㄷ 遇元音变 ㄹ），ㅡ 脱落（词干末 ㅡ.en:
Two types of irregular rules:
ㄷ irregular (some ㄷ changes to ㄹ before vowels), ㅡ deletion (the final ㅡ in the stem disappears before 아/어요).
This lesson is about the tricky part of Chapter 2—not "how to use" but "why it changes this way."
Understanding the pattern saves much more effort than rote memorization.
Chinese verbs have no phonetic changes, so these two irregular patterns are the most unfamiliar part for native Chinese speakers and need special attention.

两套变形规则独立存在：\\nㄷ 不规则影响\"听/走/问\"这类动词，ㅡ 脱落影.en: Two independent irregular rules:\nㄷ irregular affects verbs like "to listen/walk/ask," and ㅡ deletion affects adjectives like "to hurt/busy/pretty."\nBoth only trigger when followed by a vowel ending; with consonant endings like -고, the stem stays unchanged.

ㄷ 不规则：\\n遇元音词尾 ㄷ→ㄹ（듣다→들어요），但 받다/믿다 不变要记哪.en:
ㄷ irregular:
Before vowel endings, ㄷ→ㄹ (듣다→들어요), but 받다/믿다 do not change—you need to memorize which ones change and which don't.
ㅡ deletion:
After ㅡ disappears, look at the preceding vowel to decide between 아요 or 어요;
Monosyllabic stems always take 어요 (쓰다→써요).

듣다（听）和 아프다/바쁘다/예쁘다 是日常对话里出现频率极高的词。\\n掌握这.en: 듣다 (to listen) and 아프다/바쁘다/예쁘다 are extremely frequent words in everyday conversation.\nMaster this lesson and you can naturally say "I'm listening to music," "my head hurts," "I've been busy lately," and "this song is really nice," making your expressions much richer.

ㄷ不规则 + ㅡ脱落 常用词.en: ㄷ Irregular + ㅡ Deletion Common Words

完成这份练习，检验第二章前 10 课是否掌握。\\n涵盖助词、数词、否定、时间、.en: Complete this exercise to check if you've mastered the first 10 lessons of Chapter 2.\nIt covers core topics such as particles, numbers, negation, time, and irregular conjugations.

这是第二章的总复习。\\n遇到不确定的题，先回想\"这是哪节课的知识点\"，再作.en: This is a comprehensive review of Chapter 2.\nWhen you encounter a question you're unsure about, first think, "Which lesson does this concept belong to?" before answering. This habit helps reinforce memory better than guessing.

说正在做、之前一直在做.en: Saying what is happening now or what was happening before

-고 있어요 把动作拉成正在进行的状态；\\n-고 있었어요 表达过去某个时候正.en: -고 있어요 turns an action into an ongoing state;\n-고 있었어요 expresses that something was happening at a specific time in the past.\nIt's similar to "currently..." in Chinese, but Korean can also use it for continuous states like "wearing" or "holding."

这节课只有一个核心结构：\\n动词词干 + -고 있어요。\\n现在进行用 있어.en:
This lesson has one core structure:
Verb stem + -고 있어요.
Use 있어요 for present progressive and 있었어요 for past progressive.
Note that this structure only attaches to verbs, not adjectives.

-고 接续时不触发不规则变化（듣다→듣고 있어요，不变形）。\\n特殊用法：\\.en: -고 does not trigger irregular conjugations when attached (듣다→듣고 있어요, no change).\nSpecial usage:\nWear/carry verbs like 입다/쓰다/들다 + -고 있어요 express a continuous state of "wearing" or "holding," not an action in progress.

-고 있어요 是 SNS 和聊天里最自然的表达\"在听歌\"\"在看剧\"\"在.en: -고 있어요 is the most natural way on social media and in chats to say "listening to music," "watching a show," or "waiting for someone."\nThe wear/carry usage (입고 있어요/쓰고 있어요) is also very common when describing someone's appearance.

判断对错：-고 있다 的用法.en: True or False: Usage of -고 있다

说以前曾经……现在不一样了.en: Saying something happened before, but is different now

-았었/었었/였었어요 表达过去曾经有过的经历或状态，常带有\"现在可能已经不同.en: -았었/었었/였었어요 expresses a past experience or state that once existed, often carrying the nuance that "things may be different now." It adds a layer of reminiscence compared to the simple past tense. There is no exact equivalent in Chinese; think of it as "used to... (but not necessarily now)."

这节课在P1过去时基础上加一层：\\n-았어요 是普通过去，-았었어요 是\"回.en: This lesson builds on the past tense from P1 by adding an extra layer: -았어요 is the simple past, while -았었어요 is the "reminiscent past," emphasizing that the present differs from the past. The structure adds another -었어요 to the past tense ending.

变形逻辑和普通过去时完全一样（看词干末尾元音选 았/었/였），只是再叠一层 었어.en: The conjugation logic is exactly the same as the simple past tense (choose 았/었/였 based on the final vowel of the stem), just with an additional 었어요 stacked on. Note: For ordinary events that happened yesterday, use -았어요, not -았었어요 (어제 밥을 먹었어요 ✓, 먹었었어요 ✗).

\"以前喜欢过这个歌手\"\"小时候住过首尔\"\"以前经常听这首歌\"这类带着.en: Expressions like "I used to like this singer," "I lived in Seoul as a child," or "I used to listen to this song often"—those with a sense of nostalgia and change—are exactly where -았었어요 shines. It's perfect for talking about idols, sharing experiences, and reminiscing about the past.

说想做什么，以及\"那样的话\".en: Saying what you want to do, and "in that case"

-고 싶어요 表达说话人自己的愿望；\\n그러면 连接条件和结果，表示\"那么/.en: -고 싶어요 expresses the speaker's own desire; 그러면 connects a condition and result, meaning "then/in that case." -고 싶어요 is mainly used for first-person wishes; to say a third person "wants to do," you typically switch to -고 싶어하다. Unlike Chinese: In Chinese, "want to do" doesn't distinguish by person, but in Korean, first person uses 싶어요, while third person requires 싶어하다.

两块内容：①-고 싶어요（想做）动词词干直接加，非常规律；\\n②그러면（那么）.en: Two parts: ① -고 싶어요 (want to do) is added directly to the verb stem, very regular; ② 그러면 (then/if so) goes at the start of a sentence to connect two clauses, and in speech it's often shortened to 그럼.

-고 싶어요 只接动词词干，不能直接接名词（커피고 싶어요 ✗）。\\n说第三人.en: -고 싶어요 only attaches to verb stems, not directly to nouns (커피고 싶어요 ✗). To express a third person's wish, use -고 싶어하다 (친구는 가고 싶어해요). 그러면 indicates a conditional sequence, unlike 그렇지만 which is used for contrast.

-고 싶어요 是表达愿望最自然的方式说学习目标、旅行计划、购物心愿都用它。\\n.en: -고 싶어요 is the most natural way to express desires—use it for study goals, travel plans, and shopping wishes. Add 그러면/그럼 to make "if... then..." suggestions, and your conversations will flow much more smoothly.

认识ㄹ收音词的特殊变形规律.en: Learn the special conjugation pattern for words ending in ㄹ

ㄹ 不规则不是永远变化，而是遇到 ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ 开头的语尾时 ㄹ 脱落。\\n接.en: The ㄹ irregular isn't always changing—it drops only when followed by endings that start with ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ. It stays when followed by -아요/어요 or -고. Common words: 살다, 알다, 만들다, 놀다. There's no similar rule in English, so just remember "drop it before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ" and you're set.

这节课不是新句型，而是变形规则：\\nㄹ 词干在接哪些语尾时会脱落 ㄹ，在哪些语.en: This lesson isn't a new sentence pattern but a conjugation rule: which endings cause ㄹ to drop from the stem, and which ones keep it. Comparing the different forms of common words (살다/알다/만들다) is faster than memorizing the rule.

ㄹ 脱落触发条件：\\n后接语尾首字母是 ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ（如 -(으)세요、正式体.en: When ㄹ drops: if the following ending starts with ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ (e.g., -(으)세요, formal -ㅂ니다/습니다, adnominal -는). When it stays: before vowel endings (-아요/어요) or -고. Mnemonic: 살아요 (kept) / 사세요 (dropped) / 삽니다 (dropped) / 사는 (dropped).

살다/알다/만들다 是极高频词问住哪、问认不认识、说自己做的。\\n掌握 ㄹ 脱.en: 살다/알다/만들다 are super high-frequency words—used for asking where someone lives, whether they know something, or talking about what you make. Master the ㄹ drop and you won't make spelling mistakes with these words, and you'll recognize them more easily when listening.

判断对错：ㄹ不规则音变.en: True or False: ㄹ Irregular Conjugation

说\"好的我知道了\"和做选择.en: Saying "Okay, I got it" and making choices

-을/ㄹ래요 表达\"我要……/要不要……\"，比 -고 싶어요 更直接；\\n.en: -을/ㄹ래요 expresses "I will.../Do you want to...?" and is more direct than -고 싶어요;\n-겠- expresses intention, speculation, or politeness, with the most common fixed expression being 알겠어요 (I understand).\n-을/ㄹ래요 is similar to the casual "I'll..." in spoken English, while -겠- is similar to "I will/I'll take care of...".

两块内容：①-을/ㄹ래요（要做/要不要）看词干有无收音选 을래요/ㄹ래요；\\n.en: Two parts: ①-을/ㄹ래요 (will do/want to do) — choose 을래요 or ㄹ래요 based on whether the stem ends in a final consonant;\n②-겠- (intention/politeness) — for beginners, just mastering the fixed expression 알겠어요 is enough.

-을/ㄹ래요 收音规则和之前完全一样：\\n有收音接 을래요，无收音接 ㄹ래요。.en:
The final consonant rule for -을/ㄹ래요 is exactly the same as before:
Use 을래요 after a final consonant, and ㄹ래요 after no final consonant.
-겠- is added directly to the stem without considering final consonants.
Note the difference:
-고 싶어요 is an inner desire (softer), while -을/ㄹ래요 is a direct statement (more colloquial).

갈래요/먹을래요/볼래요 是朋友间最自然的邀约用语\"要去吗？\"\"要吃什么？.en: 갈래요/먹을래요/볼래요 are the most natural invitation phrases among friends: "Want to go?" "What do you want to eat?"\n알겠어요 is a response you'll use every day in class or service settings.\nAfter this lesson, your everyday conversation will flow noticeably better.

选择正确的意志表达.en: Choosing the Right Expression of Intention

问什么、哪个、什么样的.en: Asking what, which, and what kind

三个疑问词都可译成\"什么/哪\"，但用法不同：\\n무슨 问名称内容，어느 从.en: All three question words can be translated as "what/which," but they're used differently:\n무슨 asks about the name or content, 어느 chooses which one from options, and 어떤 asks about qualities or characteristics.\nIn English, "what song," "which song," and "what kind of song" correspond to these three words.

这节课三个疑问词都放在名词前面，结构一样，区别只在\"问的是什么\"。\\n记住.en: In this lesson, all three question words come before a noun, so the structure is the same—the difference is only in what you're asking about.\nRemember three typical sentences:\n무슨 뜻이에요? / 어느 나라 사람이에요? / 어떤 음식을 좋아해요?

어느 只用于疑问句，肯定句里不用（不说\"어느 노래가 좋아요\"来表达喜欢）。.en: 어느 is only used in questions; it's not used in affirmative sentences (you wouldn't say "어느 노래가 좋아요" to express liking).\nThe difference between 무슨 and 어떤:\nUse 무슨 to ask "what's it called/what is it," and 어떤 to ask "what kind/what characteristics."

这三个词是开启话题的万能钥匙\"这是什么歌\"\"你是哪国人\"\"喜欢什么样的.en: These three words are the key to starting conversations: "What song is this?" "Which country are you from?" "What kind of food do you like?"\nMaster this lesson, and you'll be able to ask more precise questions—your conversations won't rely only on "뭐예요?" anymore.

그렇지만 是明确转折\"但是\"；\\n그런데 语气更口语，可以是轻转折\"不过.en:
그렇지만 is a clear contrast "but"; 
그런데 is more colloquial, can be a soft "though" or used to advance the topic or introduce new information. 
This lesson overlaps with 그렇지만 from P2, but the focus is on the new 그런데, so make sure you understand the difference. 
It's similar to the difference between "but" and "though" in Chinese: 
그렇지만 ≈ but (formal contrast), 그런데 ≈ though (colloquial, can also shift topics).

两个连词都放在第二句句首，结构完全一样。\\n区别在语气和功能：\\n그렇지만.en: Both conjunctions go at the start of the second sentence, with identical structure. \nThe difference is in tone and function: \n그렇지만 only marks contrast, while 그런데 can also shift topics ("By the way, what does this word mean?").

判断用哪个很简单：\\n前后有明确对比关系用 그렇지만；\\n想轻松转换话题或信.en:
Deciding which to use is simple: 
Use 그렇지만 when there's a clear contrast between the two parts; 
Use 그런데 when you want to casually shift topics or introduce new information. 
In spoken Korean, 그런데 is far more common than 그렇지만 and can cover most situations.

그런데 是韩语口语里出现最频繁的连词之一用来插入新话题、提出疑问、轻轻转折。\\.en: 그런데 is one of the most frequently used conjunctions in spoken Korean—used to insert new topics, ask questions, or make a light contrast. \nOnce you learn 그런데, your conversations will flow more naturally, and you won't be limited to just "but" as a transition.

说\"所以/因此\"，连接原因结果.en: Say "so/therefore" to connect cause and result

그래서 连接原因和自然结果；\\n그러니까 也表示所以/因此，口语中常带总结、提.en: 그래서 connects a cause to its natural result; \n그러니까 also means so/therefore, but in spoken language it often carries a tone of summarizing, reminding, or advising. \nBoth correspond to "so" in Chinese, but the difference is that 그러니까 is more like "so I'm saying..."—with a stronger emphasis.

两个连词都放第二句句首，原因在前，结果在后，顺序不能反。\\n区别：\\n그래서.en: Both conjunctions go at the start of the second sentence, with the cause first and the result second—the order can't be reversed. \nThe difference: \n그래서 states a natural result, while 그러니까 often introduces a suggestion or reminder (so you should...).

原因-结果顺序固定，不能倒装（비가 와요. 그래서 집에 있어요. ✓）。\\n.en:
The cause-result order is fixed and can't be inverted (비가 와요. 그래서 집에 있어요. ✓). 
그래서 and 그러니까 are not used for contrast—use 그런데/그렇지만 for that. 
The difference between the two: 
그래서 = natural result, 그러니까 = a summary with an advisory tone.

日常生活中因为……所以……无处不在\"因为下雨所以在家\"\"因为太忙所以不能去.en: In everyday life, "because...so..." is everywhere—"because it's raining, so I'm staying home," "because I'm too busy, so I can't go." \nOnce you master 그래서, you can explain reasons, express connections, and make your conversations more logical.

说\"去做某事\"，以及提议询问.en: Saying "go to do something" and making suggestions

-(으)러 가다/오다 表达\"去/来做某事\"的目的；\\n-을/ㄹ까요? 用.en: -(으)러 가다/오다 expresses the purpose of "going/coming to do something"; -을/ㄹ까요? is used to suggest or ask for an opinion, meaning "Shall we...?" In Chinese, "go eat" is said directly, but in Korean, the purpose particle -(으)러 connects the verb with go/come.

两块内容：①-(으)러 가다/오다（去做某事）目的动词加 러/으러，后接 가요/.en: Two parts: ①-(으)러 가다/오다 (go to do something) — add 러/으러 to the purpose verb, then attach 가요/와요; ②-을/ㄹ까요? (suggestion/question) — attach to the verb stem, choosing 을/ㄹ based on whether there is a final consonant.

-(으)러 的收音规则：\\n有收音接 으러（먹으러），无收音接 러（보러）。\.en: Final consonant rule for -(으)러: with a final consonant, use 으러 (먹으러); without one, use 러 (보러). Note the difference between -(으)러 가요 (go to do) and -고 가요 (do and then go) — the former is purpose, the latter is sequence. -을/ㄹ까요 can also be used with adjectives (좋을까요?).

뭐 먹으러 갈까요？这一句几乎是韩国人约饭时的标准开场白。\\n-(으)러 가다.en: 뭐 먹으러 갈까요? is almost the standard opening line when Koreans plan a meal together. Combining -(으)러 가다 and -을/ㄹ까요 lets you invite, suggest, and express purpose — you'll use it all the time in daily conversation.

判断对错：-(으)러 和 -을까요 的用法.en: True or False: Usage of -(으)러 and -을까요

-은/ㄴ 후에 表达\"做完……之后\"；\\n-기 전에 表达\"做……之前\.en: -은/ㄴ 후에 expresses "after doing..."; -기 전에 expresses "before doing...". Using them together lets you clearly express time order, perfect for study plans, schedules, and diaries. Note: -기 전에 simply adds 기 regardless of final consonants, making it easier than -은/ㄴ 후에. In Chinese, "after/before" goes directly after the verb, but Korean requires correct verb endings — especially the final consonant rule for -은/ㄴ 후에, which is a challenge that doesn't exist in Chinese.

两个时间表达结构不同：\\n-은/ㄴ 후에 接在动词变形后（要看收音），-기 전.en: The two time expressions have different structures: -은/ㄴ 후에 attaches to a conjugated verb (depending on the final consonant), while -기 전에 directly attaches 기 to the stem without needing to consider final consonants. Remember this difference first, and the conjugations won't get confusing.

후에 接续：\\n有收音→은 후에（먹은 후에），无收音→ㄴ 후에（본 후에）。.en:
후에 attachment: 
With a final consonant → 은 후에 (먹은 후에), without a final consonant → ㄴ 후에 (본 후에).
전에 attachment: 
Always -기 전에, regardless of the final consonant.
Common mistake: 
먹은 전에 ✗, you must say 먹기 전에.

日记、学习计划、日常习惯\"吃饭后学习\"\"睡觉前复习\"\"听歌前看歌词\".en:
Diaries, study plans, daily habits—"study after eating," "review before sleeping," "read lyrics before listening to songs." These time-order expressions are used every day.
Master this lesson and your Korean diary will instantly sound more natural.

完成这份练习，检验第三章前 10 课是否掌握。\\n涵盖进行时、经历回顾、愿望、.en:
Complete this practice to check if you've mastered the first 10 lessons of Chapter 3.
It covers core points such as the progressive tense, past experience, wishes, ㄹ irregular verbs, intentions and choices, question words, connectors, purpose expressions, and time order.

这是第三章的总复习。\\n第三章的核心是\"时态扩展\"和\"句子连接\"进行时.en:
This is the overall review of Chapter 3.
The core of Chapter 3 is "tense expansion" and "sentence connection"—progressive, past experience, wishes, purpose, and order are all tools that turn single sentences into complex ones.
Keep this main thread in mind while solving the problems.

连接两个动作，说原因和顺序.en: Connect two actions to express reason and sequence

两个连接形式功能不同：\\n-고 是中性连接（做A然后做B），-아/어/여서 是.en:
The two connectors have different functions:
-고 is a neutral connector (do A then do B), -아/어/여서 is a causal connector (because A, so B).
Structurally, both attach to the stem of the preceding verb, and the following clause is stated normally.

-고 接续最简单直接去掉 다 加 고，-고 以辅音开头，不触发任何不规则变化（ㄷ.en:
-고 attaches by simply dropping 다 and adding 고. Since -고 starts with a consonant, it doesn't trigger any irregular changes (ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ, 르, ㅡ, ㄹ are all unaffected). When attaching to an already-conjugated past tense form, keep the changed result (들었고).
-아/어/여서 conjugates the same way as -아요/어요: 
If the last vowel of the stem is ㅏ or ㅗ → add 아서, otherwise → add 어서, and 하다 → 해서.
Note: 
Sentences using -아/어/여서 to express reason shouldn't be followed by a command.

这两个连接形式是韩语表达的骨架\"喝完咖啡再学\"\"因为发音快所以难\"\"因.en: These two connective forms are the backbone of Korean expression: "drink coffee and then study," "it's hard because pronunciation is fast," "rest because I have a headache" — almost every compound sentence uses them.\nMaster this lesson and your Korean will go from "choppy phrases" to "flowing sentences."

说必须做，或请别人别做.en: Say what must be done, or ask someone not to do something

-아/어/여야 해요 / 돼요 表达\"必须、应该、得……\"；\\n-지 마세.en: -아/어/여야 해요 / 돼요 expresses "must, should, have to..."; \n-지 마세요 expresses "please don't...". \n-아/어/여야 해요 corresponds to "have to/must..." and -지 마세요 to "please don't..." — both are extremely common in everyday speech.

两块内容：①必须做（-아/어/여야 해요/돼요）变形和 -아요/어요 一样，再加.en: Two parts: ① Must do (-아/어/여야 해요/돼요) — conjugate the same way as -아요/어요, then add 야 해요/돼요; \n② Please don't (-지 마세요) — attach 지 마세요 directly to the stem, no need to consider the final consonant.

变形重点：\\n하다 动词→해야 해요（공부해야 해요），不是 하야 해요。\\.en:
Conjugation points: 
하다 verbs → 해야 해요 (공부해야 해요), not 하야 해요. 
ㄷ irregular verbs trigger before -아/어야 (듣다→들어야 해요). 
돼요 and 해요 mean the same; 돼요 is more colloquial. 
-지 마세요 carries an imperative tone that -지 않아요 doesn't have — don't mix them up.

必须做的事（复习、练习、准时到）和请求别人不要做（别担心、别忘了）这两种表达在学.en: Expressing things you must do (review, practice, arrive on time) and asking others not to do something (don't worry, don't forget) appear everywhere — in study check-ins, daily conversation, and service settings.\nAfter this lesson, you'll be able to make requests and express obligations.

说花了多长时间、多少钱.en: Say how long something takes or how much money it costs

걸려요 表示花费时间；\\n-는 데 돈이 들어요 表示做某事花钱。\\n和中文.en: 걸려요 indicates time spent; -는 데 돈이 들어요 indicates spending money on something. In Chinese, "took thirty minutes" or "costs a lot" correspond to Korean verbs 걸리다 (for time) and 들다 (for money), which cannot be mixed up.

两块内容：①걸려요（花时间）时间词做主语，结构是\"时间 + 걸려요\"；\\n.en: Two parts: ①걸려요 (time spent) takes a time word as the subject, structure is "time + 걸려요"; ②돈이 들어요 (money spent) combines with -는 데 to say "spending money on doing something." The subjects differ: for 걸려요, the subject is time; for 들어요, the subject is 돈.

걸리다 只用于时间，不能说花钱（花钱用 돈이 들어요）。\\n-는 데 是动词的.en: 걸리다 is only used for time, not for money (use 돈이 들어요 for money). -는 데 is the present tense modifier form of a verb + 데, meaning "the act of doing..." Time readings: minutes use Sino-Korean numbers (삼십 분), hours use native Korean numbers (두 시간).

\"从家到学校要多久\"\"去演唱会很花钱\"这类描述日常花费的表达，出行、购物.en: Expressions like "How long does it take from home to school?" or "Going to a concert costs a lot" are used in daily life when describing time and money costs—needed for travel, shopping, and planning. With this lesson, you can accurately describe time and money expenses.

说话时加自然的铺垫语气.en: Adds a natural, softening tone when speaking

-은/ㄴ/는데요 是口语常用的铺垫表达，带有\"是这样，不过……\"的语气，用于.en: -은/ㄴ/는데요 is a common conversational filler that carries a nuance of "well, it's like this, but..." It's used for contrast, explanation, or to lead into what follows. Chinese has no exact equivalent—it's more like a discourse marker that makes sentences sound softer and more natural, less direct.

变形规则按词性分三类：\\n动词→-는데요，形容词→-은/ㄴ데요（按收音），名词.en: Conjugation rules fall into three categories by part of speech: verbs → -는데요, adjectives → -은/ㄴ데요 (depending on the final consonant), nouns → 인데요. The challenge at this stage isn't the conjugation itself, but understanding what this marker does—it's a lead-in, not a contrast word.

形容词的变形：\\n有收音→은데요（좋은데요），无收音→ㄴ데요（예쁜데요）。\\.en:
Adjective conjugation:
With a final consonant → 은데요 (좋은데요), without a final consonant → ㄴ데요 (예쁜데요).
ㅂ irregular applies here:
어렵다→어려운데요.
있다/없다 use -는데요 (same as verbs).
Past tense uniformly uses 았/었는데요.

-는데요 是让韩语听起来\"像韩国人说的\"的关键语气词\"我在学习呢\"\"这.en: -는데요 is the key ending that makes Korean sound "like a native speaker"—"I'm studying" "This song is nice, but..." "I'm a student...".\nMaster this, and your expressions will become softer and more natural, no longer just dry statements.

把动作变名词，把形容词变副词.en: Turn actions into nouns and adjectives into adverbs

-는 것 直接接动词词干，形容词名词化是 -ㄴ/은 것（后续课程）。\\n-게.en: -는 것 attaches directly to the verb stem; adjective nominalization uses -ㄴ/은 것 (in a later lesson).\n-게 attaches directly to the adjective stem, but note:\n빠르다, 많다, 높다 have their own dedicated adverbs (빨리/많이/높이), so use those instead of -게.

\"学韩语这件事很有意思\"\"把句子写得简单一点\"\"快速读歌词\"-는 것.en: "Learning Korean is interesting," "write the sentence a bit more simply," "read the lyrics quickly"—-는 것 and -게 appear frequently in study check-ins, fan activities, and everyday expressions.\nMaster these two tools, and you can express yourself more precisely.

N보다 表示\"比……\"；\\n에 비해서 表示\"和……相比\"（更书面）。.en: N보다 means "more than...";\n에 비해서 means "compared to..." (more formal).\nJust like in Chinese, Korean comparative sentences follow the structure "A is more... than B." 보다 is equivalent to Chinese "比" and attaches directly after the comparison standard.

这节课两个比较结构：①보다（口语比较）直接接在名词后，配合 더 加强；\\n②에.en: This lesson covers two comparative structures: ① 보다 (colloquial comparison) attaches directly to a noun, and can be strengthened with 더;\n② 에 비해서 (formal comparison) is better suited for analysis and explanation.\nBoth can mean "more than...", but they differ in register.

보다 直接贴名词后，无需考虑收音。\\n더 可加可不加，加了更强调\"更\"。\.en:
보다 attaches directly to nouns without considering the final consonant.
더 can be added or omitted; adding it emphasizes "more."
Note the dual role of 보다: as a verb it means "to see," while as a comparison particle it means "than," distinguished by its position in the sentence.
에 비해서/비하면/비하여 are three forms of the same expression.

比较两首歌、两个语言的难度、两个地方的特点보다 是日常表达里用频率最高的比较词。.en: Comparing two songs, the difficulty of two languages, or the characteristics of two places—보다 is the most frequently used comparison word in everyday speech.\nAfter this lesson, you'll be able to accurately say "sounds better than..." or "harder than yesterday."

说用什么工具、以什么身份.en: Saying what tool you use or what role you take

(으)로 是多义助词：\\n表示工具/语言、方向、身份结果。\\n有收音用 으로.en:
(으)로 is a multi-purpose particle:
It indicates tools/language, direction, identity, or result.
Use 으로 after a final consonant, and 로 after no consonant or a ㄹ final consonant.
Expressions like "say it in Korean," "go to the right," and "pay with a credit card" all rely on (으)로.

(으)로 有四种用法：\\n方向（往哪走）、工具/语言（用什么说/做）、变化结果.en: (으)로 has four uses:\ndirection (where to go), tool/language (what to say/do with), change result (what it becomes), and identity (as what).\nThe structure is the same—it attaches to a noun—and context determines the meaning.

收音规则有个例外：\\nㄹ 收音不接 으로，直接接 로（지하철로 / 서울로）。.en:
There's an exception to the final consonant rule:
ㄹ final consonants do not take 으로; they directly take 로 (지하철로 / 서울로).
Distinguish 에 from (으)로:
에 means "arriving at a destination," while (으)로 means "moving toward a direction"—학교에 가요 (go to school) vs 오른쪽으로 가요 (go to the right).

\"用韩语说\"\"往右转\"\"用相机拍\"\"换大号\"(으)로 是你在韩国.en: "Say it in Korean," "turn right," "take a photo with the camera," "change to a larger size"—(으)로 is a particle you can't avoid when asking for directions, shopping, or communicating in Korea.\nMaster this lesson, and you'll naturally produce expressions like "with/using/toward/as."

(이)나 连接名词表示\"或者\"；\\n-거나 连接动作表示\"或者做……\".en: (이)나 connects nouns to mean "or"; -거나 connects actions to mean "or do...". In Chinese, "coffee or tea" and "listen to music or watch a show" — the former uses (이)나, the latter uses -거나. Just remember by noun vs. verb.

两块内容：①(이)나（名词之间的或者）按收音选 이나/나；\\n②-거나（动作之.en: Two parts: ① (이)나 (or between nouns) — choose 이나/나 based on final consonant; ② -거나 (or between actions) — attach directly to the verb stem, no final consonant rule. Expressing choices is one of the most basic needs in daily conversation.

(이)나 的收音规则和 이/가 完全一样：\\n有收音→이나（책이나），无收音→.en: The final consonant rule for (이)나 is exactly the same as 이/가: with a final consonant → 이나 (책이나), without → 나 (커피나). -거나 attaches directly to the stem, so the rule is consistent. Note that (이)나 also has another use: meaning "at least/even" (밥이나 먹어요 = just eat something), with a softer tone.

\"休息日听歌或者看剧\"\"喝咖啡还是茶\"\"无聊就刷刷手机\"(이)나/-.en: "On a day off, listen to music or watch a show," "coffee or tea," "scroll through your phone when bored" — (이)나/-거나 are extremely common when describing daily choices and habits. Master this lesson to describe your routine more naturally.

说从谁那里得到，礼貌称呼人.en: Say "from someone" and politely address people

에게서/한테서 表示\"从谁那里\"；\\n씨 是人名后的礼貌称呼；\\n짜리.en: 에게서/한테서 means "from someone"; 씨 is a polite title after a person's name; 짜리 indicates a price/age/denomination attribute. These three points are independent, but all are very practical details in everyday Korean. In Chinese, "from a friend" is one structure, but Korean distinguishes by register: 에게서 (written) and 한테서 (spoken).

三块内容：①에게서/한테서（从谁那里收到/听说）和 에게/한테 方向相反；\\n.en: Three parts: ① 에게서/한테서 (received/heard from someone) — opposite direction to 에게/한테; ② 씨 (title usage) — attaches to the given name, not the surname; ③ 짜리 (attribute modifier) — attaches to a price/quantity to modify a noun.

에게서/한테서 的方向逻辑：\\n에게/한테=给出去，에게서/한테서=从那里收进.en: Direction logic for 에게서/한테서: 에게/한테 = giving out, 에게서/한테서 = receiving in from there. 씨 usage: 김민준 씨 (full name + 씨) or 민준 씨 (given name + 씨), but you cannot say 김 씨 (surname only). 짜리 attaches directly after the number.

\"从朋友那里收到礼物\"\"从老师那里学到的\"\"买了一万韩元的票\"这三个.en: "Received a gift from a friend," "learned from a teacher," "bought a 10,000-won ticket" — these three expressions are common in shopping, conversation, and introducing people. 씨 is the most polite way Koreans address someone in daily life.

学会基本敬语，说话更有礼貌.en: Learn basic honorifics to speak more politely

-(으)세요 是最基础敬语请求形式；\\n部分特殊敬语词（드세요/계세요/말씀하.en:
-(으)세요 is the most basic honorific request form;
Some special honorific words (드세요/계세요/말씀하세요/주무세요) need to be memorized as whole words.
Korean honorifics are a cultural necessity—you must use them with elders, service staff, and strangers; not using them can come across as rude.
Unlike Chinese:
Chinese relies on the word "please" to express politeness, while Korean directly changes the verb ending. Honorifics are a grammatical requirement, not an optional polite word.

两块内容：①-(으)세요（敬语请求）已在P2学过，这节课补充更多用法和场景；\\.en: Two parts: ①-(으)세요 (honorific request) was already covered in P2; this lesson adds more uses and scenarios;\n②Special honorific words: 먹다→드세요, 있다→계세요, 자다→주무세요—these need to be memorized as whole words and cannot be derived from regular verb conjugation.

-(으)세요 变形和P2完全一样（有收音→으세요，无收音→세요）。\\n特殊敬语.en:
The -(으)세요 conjugation is exactly the same as in P2 (with a final consonant → 으세요, without → 세요).
There are only a few special honorific words; memorize them all:
먹다/마시다→드세요, 자다→주무세요, 말하다→말씀하세요.
있다 has two categories: "to be/exist" (with a person as subject) → 계세요 (아버지가 계세요); "to have/possess" → 있으세요 (질문이 있으세요?).
These words follow no pattern—you just have to memorize them.

在韩国咖啡店、地铁、见朋友父母随处都需要用到敬语。\\n드세요（请吃/请喝）和.en: You'll need honorifics everywhere in Korea—at coffee shops, on the subway, and when meeting your friends' parents.\n드세요 (please eat/drink) and 계세요 (to be) are the most frequently used special honorific words.\nAfter this lesson, you'll be able to speak naturally in polite situations without sounding out of place.

判断对错：敬语的用法.en: True or False: Usage of Honorifics

综合运用第四章 L01-L10 所学语法：\\n动作连接与原因（-고/-아서）、.en: Comprehensively apply the grammar from Chapter 4, Lessons L01–L10:\nAction connection and reason (-고/-아서), obligation and prohibition (-아야 해요/-지 마세요), spending time/money (걸리다/들다), softening tone (-는데요), nominalization and adverbialization (-는 것/-게), comparison (보다/에 비해서), tool/direction/identity ((으)로), choice ((이)나/-거나), source and address (에게서/씨), and basic honorifics (-(으)세요).

这是第四章的总复习。\\n第四章的主线是\"表达更精细\"怎么连句、怎么说义务、.en: This is the comprehensive review for Chapter 4.\nThe main theme of Chapter 4 is "expressing more precisely" — how to connect sentences, how to express obligation, how to compare, and how to speak politely.\nWhen solving problems, think about the "expressive function" behind each grammar point, not just memorizing the forms.

-(으)면 表示\"如果……\"的条件；\\n-(으)려면 表示\"想要做……的.en: -(으)면 expresses the condition "if...";\n-(으)려면 expresses "if you want to do...", and the following clause often contains a suggestion or request.\n-(으)면 corresponds to "if...then..." in English, while -(으)려면 corresponds to "if you want to..., you should...". These are the most core conditional structures in Chapter 5.

两个条件结构共用一套收音规则：\\n有收音→으면/으려면，无收音/ㄹ收音→면/려.en:
Both conditional structures share the same batchim (final consonant) rules:
With a batchim → -으면/-으려면, without a batchim or with ㄹ batchim → -면/-려면.
The difference is in meaning:
-(으)면 is a general condition, while -(으)려면 is a condition based on a goal, and the following clause often pairs with -야 해요 or -세요.

ㄹ 收音直接接 -면（살면/알면），不脱落 ㄹ。\\n不规则在此正常触发：\\n.en:
A ㄹ batchim directly attaches to -면 (살면/알면), and the ㄹ is not dropped.
Irregular rules apply normally here:
듣다→들으면, 춥다→추우면, 어렵다→어려우면.
-(으)려면 is a shortened form of -(으)려고 하면, and the following clause is suitable for commands or obligation sentences.

\"如果有时间就去\"\"想把韩语学好就要每天练习\"条件句是日常对话里最常用的.en: "If you have time, go" "If you want to get good at Korean, you should practice every day" — conditional sentences are among the most commonly used sentence patterns in daily conversation.\nMaster this lesson and you can give advice, express plans, and describe "if..." situations.

안/-지 않다 表示主观\"不做\"；\\n못/-지 못하다 表示客观\"不能/.en: 안/-지 않다 expresses a subjective "not doing";\n못/-지 못하다 expresses an objective "cannot do / unable to do", often due to ability or circumstances.\nThis distinction is not obvious in Chinese, but in Korean you must clearly differentiate — "I don't drink coffee" and "I can't drink coffee" are completely different expressions.

两套否定各有短形和长形：\\n안/못（短形，口语常用）和 -지 않다/-지 못하.en:
Each negation has a short form and a long form:
안/못 (short form, common in speech) and -지 않다/-지 못하다 (long form, more complete).
The short form goes directly before the verb, while the long form attaches to the stem followed by 지.
Note that 못 cannot be used with adjectives.

하다 动词的否定要把 안/못 插在 하다 前面：\\n공부 안 해요，不是 안.en:
To negate a 하다 verb, place 안/못 before 하다: 
공부 안 해요, not 안 공부해요.
못 cannot be used with adjectives (날씨가 못 좋아요 ✗→안 좋아요 ✓).
Key distinction: 
Use 안 for voluntary refusal, and 못 when conditions/ability don't allow it.

\"我不吃辣\"\"因为过敏所以不能喝\"\"发音太快跟不上\"\\n안 和 못.en: "I don't eat spicy food" "I can't drink because of allergies" "I can't keep up because the pronunciation is too fast"\nDistinguishing between 안 and 못 is a very practical skill in daily conversation, helping you express yourself more accurately and avoid misunderstandings.

说打算做什么，大概会怎样.en: Express what you plan to do or what will probably happen

-(으)려고 해요 表示\"打算/准备做某事\"；\\n아마 -을/ㄹ 거예요.en:
-(으)려고 해요 means "plan to / intend to do something";
아마 -을/ㄹ 거예요 expresses a guess of "will probably...".
The former is an extension of the future tense -을/ㄹ 거예요, which says "will do," while this lesson's -(으)려고 해요 emphasizes "having a plan/intention."
In Chinese, "plan to go" and "will go" are distinguished by separate words, but Korean uses different endings attached directly to the verb stem.

两块内容：①-(으)려고 해요（计划/意图）有收音接 으려고，无收音接 려고；\.en: Two parts: ①-(으)려고 해요 (plan/intention) — attach 으려고 after a final consonant, 려고 after no final consonant;\n②아마 -을/ㄹ 거예요 (guess) — you've already learned -을/ㄹ 거예요, and adding 아마 means "probably/maybe."

-(으)려고 해요 的主语必须是有意志的人/动物，天气等无意志主语不能用（날씨가.en:
The subject of -(으)려고 해요 must be a person or animal with will; subjects without will like weather cannot be used (날씨가 따뜻하려고 해요 ✗).
Strength of guess: 
갈 거예요 (will go) → 아마 갈 거예요 (will probably go).
ㅂ irregular trigger: 
어렵다→어려울 거예요.

\"今天打算复习单词\"\"打算去演唱会\"\"票大概会很贵\"计划和推测是学习.en: "I plan to review vocabulary today" "I plan to go to the concert" "The tickets will probably be expensive" — plans and guesses are the most common expressions in study journals, chats, and discussions about the future.\nMastering this lesson lets you state your own plans and also guess what others are up to.

이/가 的收音规则和主格助词相同：\\n有收音→이 아니에요，无收音→가 아니에.en:
The final consonant rule for 이/가 is the same as for the subject particle: 
with final consonant → 이 아니에요, without final consonant → 가 아니에요. 
In -는 게 아니라, 게 is a colloquial contraction of 것이. 
Note: 
아니에요 can end a sentence alone, but 아니라 must be followed by B예요 to provide the correct answer.

\"这不是咖啡而是茶\"\"不是背单词而是要理解\"\"我不是老师，我是学生\".en: "This isn't coffee but tea," "It's not memorizing words but understanding," "I'm not a teacher, I'm a student"—correcting misunderstandings, clarifying identity, and stating the truth are very common in daily conversation. \nBy learning this lesson, you can more confidently say "it's not like that."

动词、形容词的冠词形.en: Adnominal Forms of Verbs and Adjectives

用动作和状态来修饰名词.en: Modify nouns with actions and states

动词/形容词加冠词形后置于名词前：\\n现在动作用 -는，形容词用 -은/ㄴ，未.en: Verbs/adjectives take an adnominal form and are placed before the noun: \npresent action uses -는, adjectives use -은/ㄴ, future/incomplete uses -을/ㄹ. \nIn Chinese, adjectives can directly modify nouns ("difficult grammar" "studying person"), but in Korean, you need to transform the word and add a specific ending to place it before a noun.

动词 -는 不看收音，统一接 는。\\n形容词 -은/ㄴ 看收音：\\n有收音→.en:
For verbs, -는 is used regardless of final consonant—always attach 는. 
For adjectives, -은/ㄴ depends on the final consonant: 
with final consonant → 은, without → ㄴ. 
-을/ㄹ depends on the final consonant: 
with final consonant → 을, without → ㄹ. 
Note: 있다/없다 use -는 (있는/없는), same as verbs. 
ㅂ irregular triggers: 
어렵다→어려운.

\"现在听的歌\"\"学习韩语的人\"\"明天要去的地方\"冠词形是韩语里使用频.en: "The song I'm listening to now," "people studying Korean," "the place I'll go tomorrow"—adnominal forms are extremely high-frequency structures in Korean, used in almost every complex sentence. \nBy mastering this lesson, you can describe things, modify nouns, and greatly enrich your expression.

请别人帮忙，或用\"对吧\"确认.en: Asking for help, or confirming with "right?"

-아/어/여 주세요 表示\"请帮我……\"；\\n-지요? 表示确认语气\"….en:
-아/어/여 주세요 means "please do (something) for me";
-지요? expresses a confirming tone "...right? ...isn't it?", often shortened to -죠? in speech.
-아/어/여 주세요 is the most common polite way to make requests in Korean—used in restaurants, classrooms, and service settings.
In Chinese, "please help me do" relies on separate words like "帮/请," but Korean embeds "help" into the ending 주세요, which cannot be separated out.

两块内容：①-아/어/여 주세요（请帮我做）变形和 -아요/어요 一样，加 주세.en: Two parts: ① -아/어/여 주세요 (please do for me) conjugates like -아요/어요, then adds 주세요;\n② -지요?/-죠? (confirming tone) attaches directly to the stem regardless of the final consonant, used to seek agreement or confirmation.

-아/어/여 주세요 变形：\\n词干末元音 ㅏ/ㅗ→아 주세요，其他→어 주세.en:
-아/어/여 주세요 conjugation:
If the stem's last vowel is ㅏ/ㅗ → 아 주세요; otherwise → 어 주세요; 하다 → 해 주세요.
-지요? is almost always shortened to -죠? in speech.
Note:
주세요 is a request to the listener, while 주다 is used for a third party (친구한테 선물을 줘요).

\"请慢点说\"\"请再说一遍\"\"这首歌很好听吧？\"-아/어/여 주세요.en: "Please speak slowly," "Please say it again," "This song is really nice, right?" -아/어/여 주세요 is used whenever you need help, and -죠? is the most natural tone for sharing feelings or confirming information.\nAfter this lesson, your conversations will flow more smoothly and naturally.

读电话号码，说具体时间.en: Reading phone numbers and stating specific times

电话号码用汉字数词逐个读；\\n时间点用 에，时间范围用 부터…까지。\\n这节.en:
Phone numbers are read digit by digit using Sino-Korean numbers;
Specific times use 에, and time ranges use 부터…까지.
This lesson integrates the time knowledge from P2—number reading, time particles 에/부터/까지 all together.
Unlike Chinese:
Chinese uses different prepositions for "at three" and "from three to five," while Korean uses 에 for specific times and 부터…까지 for ranges, with clear division of roles.

三块内容：①电话号码读法（汉字数词逐位读，0读 공）；\\n②시간+에（在某个时.en: Three parts: ① How to read phone numbers (Sino-Korean numerals read digit by digit, 0 is read as 공); ② 시간+에 (doing something at a specific time); ③ 부터…까지 (a range from one time to another). A specific time point and a time range are two different expressions and cannot be mixed.

时间点用 에（세 시에 만나요），时间范围用 부터/까지（세 시부터 다섯 시까.en: Use 에 for a specific time point (세 시에 만나요), and use 부터/까지 for a time range (세 시부터 다섯 시까지). 0 in phone numbers is read as 공, not 영. 시 (hour) uses native Korean numerals, while 분 (minute) uses Sino-Korean numerals, same as learned in P2—this lesson reinforces that.

\"下午三点见\"\"课程从十点到十一点\"\"我的电话是010-xxxx-xx.en: "See you at 3 PM," "The class runs from 10 to 11," "My number is 010-xxxx-xxxx"—making plans, talking about schedules, and leaving contact info are situations you'll encounter every day. Master this lesson and you'll handle time-related conversations in Korea smoothly.

说坐什么交通工具去/来.en: Saying you go/come by a certain mode of transportation

을/를 타다 表示乘坐；\\n타고 가다/오다 表示坐着去/来；\\n(으)로.en: 을/를 타다 means to ride; 타고 가다/오다 means to go/come by riding; (으)로 가다/오다 means to go/come using a certain mode of transportation. The three expressions are similar in meaning, but differ in emphasis: 타고 emphasizes the action of "getting on and then going," while (으)로 emphasizes "using this method." In Chinese, "坐地铁去" (go by subway) is three separate words, but in Korean you must choose between two different structures, 타고 or (으)로, and you also need to check whether there's a final consonant to pick 으로 or 로.

三个表达方式：①타요（单独说乘坐）；\\n②타고 가요/와요（坐上后去/来，强调.en: Three expressions: ① 타요 (saying ride alone); ② 타고 가요/와요 (get on and then go/come, emphasizing continuous action); ③ (으)로 가요/와요 (go/come by a certain method, more concise). In everyday speech, both 타고 and (으)로 are common and can be used interchangeably.

타고 가다 中的 타고 是 타다+-고 的连接形（已学）。\\n(으)로 的收音.en: In 타고 가다, 타고 is the connective form of 타다 + -고 (already learned). The rule for (으)로: with a final consonant → 으로; without a final consonant or with ㄹ → 로 (버스로/지하철로). 걸어서 가요 (go on foot) is an exception—walking doesn't use 타다, but 걸어서.

\"坐地铁去公司\"\"坐飞机去韩国\"\"坐公交去学校\"说出行方式是日常对话.en: "Go to work by subway," "fly to Korea," "take the bus to school"—describing how you get around is one of the most basic daily conversation topics. Master this lesson and you'll describe transportation smoothly, and asking for directions or answering in Korea will be no problem.

说换乘、中途转车.en: Talk about transferring or changing vehicles

갈아타다 表示换乘；\\n을/를 갈아타다 强调换乘对象；\\n(으)로 갈아타.en:
갈아타다 means to transfer/change vehicles.
을/를 갈아타다 emphasizes the vehicle being transferred to;
(으)로 갈아타다 emphasizes what you are changing to;
A에서 B로 갈아타다 means transferring from A to B.
갈아타다 is an extension of 타다 (to ride), where 갈아 means "to change," so together it means "to change and ride/transfer."
Unlike in Chinese: 
In Chinese, "transfer to the subway" is a direct combination, but in Korean, particles are needed to distinguish "which line you're transferring to" (을/를) and "what you're changing into" ((으)로), making the expression more precise.

갈아타다 的助词选择和 타다 一样：\\n宾语位置用 을/를，方向/工具位置用.en:
The particle choice for 갈아타다 is the same as 타다: 
Use 을/를 for the object position, and (으)로 for the direction/vehicle position.
Use 에서 for the starting point (버스에서), and (으)로 for the destination (지하철로).
Talking about the number of transfers: 
두 번 갈아타야 해요 (I need to transfer twice).

\"在这里换乘2号线\"\"从公交换地铁\"\"要换几次\"问路和乘车时这类表达.en: Expressions like "transfer to Line 2 here," "change from bus to subway," and "how many transfers do I need" are essential when asking for directions or riding public transport.\nYou'll use these when traveling in Korea or transferring on the subway.\nCombined with the previous lesson, your travel conversations will be complete.

说做着做着发生了变化.en: Talk about something changing while doing an action

-다가 表示在做某动作的过程中发生变化、中断或切换，相当于\"做着做着……\"。.en: -다가 indicates that while doing an action, something changes, gets interrupted, or switches, equivalent to "while doing..." or "in the middle of..." in English.\nExpressions like "fell asleep while studying" or "cried while watching" — where something changes mid-action — are expressed with -다가 in Korean.

结构非常简单：\\n动词词干直接加 -다가，不看收音，后句说发生的变化或结果。\.en:
The structure is very simple: 
Add -다가 directly to the verb stem, regardless of the final consonant, and the following clause states the change or result.
Note the difference between -다가 and -고: 
-고 means "finish A, then do B," while -다가 means "while doing A (not finished), B happens."

-다가 直接接词干，无变形，不规则也不触发。\\n关键是含义前句动作必须是\"正.en:
-다가 attaches directly to the verb stem with no changes, and irregular verbs are not triggered.
The key is the meaning: the preceding action must be "in progress/incomplete," and the following clause is the change that happens mid-way.
It can be shortened to -다: 
공부하다 잠들었어요.

\"追剧追着追着哭了\"\"学习学着学着睡着了\"\"走着走着迷路了\"这类\".en: Descriptions like "cried while binge-watching a show," "fell asleep while studying," or "got lost while walking" — these "while doing" expressions are very natural when telling stories or chatting about daily experiences.\nMastering -다가 will noticeably improve your Korean narration skills.

综合运用第五章 L01-L10 所学语法：\\n条件、否定、计划推测、纠正、冠词.en: Comprehensively apply the grammar from Chapter 5, Lessons L01-L10: conditions, negation, plans and speculation, corrections, adnominal forms, asking for confirmation, transportation, transfers, and action transitions.

这是第五章的总复习。\\n第五章的主线是\"表达更立体\"条件假设、否定辨析、修.en: This is the overall review for Chapter 5. The main theme of Chapter 5 is "expressing more richly"—conditions, hypotheses, distinguishing negations, modifying nouns, and travel/transportation—to help you move from single sentences to complex situations. As you solve the problems, think about which real-life scenarios each grammar point would appear in.

说\"我来做\"，也表达共情感叹.en: Say "I'll do it" and express empathetic exclamations

-을/ㄹ게요 表示说话人的意志或承诺，主语一般是第一人称；\\n-겠군요 听到对.en: -을/ㄹ게요 expresses the speaker's intention or promise, and the subject is generally first person. -겠군요 is used when you hear what the other person said and then make a guess about a possible situation or feeling; it's common in spoken language. It's similar to the Chinese "我来做" (I'll do it), but Korean -을/ㄹ게요 carries a nuance of "considering the other person and taking initiative," making it more polite than just saying "I do it."

这节课学两个表达：① -을/ㄹ게요（我来做/我会做，向对方承诺）；\\n② -겠.en: In this lesson, you'll learn two expressions: ① -을/ㄹ게요 (I'll do it / I will do it, promising the other person); ② -겠군요 (I see, guessing and exclaiming about the other person's situation). The former emphasizes "my intention," while the latter emphasizes "my empathy for you." Both are common spoken sentence endings.

-을/ㄹ게요 的收音规则与 -을/ㄹ 거예요 相同：\\n有收音→을게요，无收音.en: The batchim (final consonant) rules for -을/ㄹ게요 are the same as for -을/ㄹ 거예요: if there's a batchim, use -을게요; if there's no batchim or the batchim is ㄹ, use -ㄹ게요. Key restriction: the subject must be first person (저/나); you can't say "you will do it" or "he will do it." -겠군요 attaches directly to the verb stem, and for past speculation, add -았/었겠군요.

\"我来拿\"\"不用担心我来帮你\"\"你一定很辛苦吧\"\"当时一定很开心吧.en: "I'll carry it," "Don't worry, I'll help you," "You must be so tired," "You must have been so happy then"—these two expressions appear frequently among friends, in the workplace, and in service settings. -을/ㄹ게요 lets you take initiative, and -겠군요 lets you show empathy; both are polite expressions that make the other person feel cared for.

比\"吗？\"更温柔的问法.en: A softer way to ask questions than "吗?"

-나요?/-은/ㄴ가요? 是 -아/어/여요?의 疑问形式，比直接疑问更自然柔和.en: -나요?/-은/ㄴ가요? are the question forms of -아/어/여요?, sounding more natural and gentle than direct questions, commonly used in spoken language;\n-ㅂ니다만/습니다만 has the same meaning as -지만, "although... but," used in formal situations or where politeness is required.\nIn Chinese, asking "Have you eaten?" has a neutral tone, while Korean -나요? adds a soft nuance, making the question sound more considerate and less forceful.

这节课学\"更礼貌的问法\"和\"正式场合的转折\"。\\n-나요? 适合动词，.en: This lesson covers "more polite question forms" and "formal transitions."\n-나요? is used with verbs, and -은/ㄴ가요? with adjectives; both are gentler than a direct question.\n-ㅂ니다만/습니다만 is the formal version of "but," often seen in polite refusals or explanations in service settings.

-나요? 直接接词干，动词和形容词都可用，不看收音。\\n-은/ㄴ가요? 只用于.en:
-나요? attaches directly to the stem and works with both verbs and adjectives, regardless of the final consonant.
-은/ㄴ가요? is only for adjectives:
With a final consonant → 은가요?, without → ㄴ가요?.
-ㅂ니다만:
Stem with final consonant → 습니다만, without → ㅂ니다만.
Note: 이다 → 입니다만.

\"请问你吃过韩国料理吗？\"\"您方便现在接听电话吗？\"\"非常抱歉，但现在.en: "Have you tried Korean food?" "Are you available to take a call right now?" "I'm very sorry, but there are no seats available at the moment." Customer service, surveys, and first-time greetings frequently use these expressions.\nMastering -나요? and -ㅂ니다만 will instantly make your Korean sound more polished.

아직 是副词，修饰后面的句子或动词，表示\"仍然（没）……，还（没）……\"，常.en: 아직 is an adverb that modifies the following sentence or verb, meaning "still (not), yet (not)," often used with negative expressions;\n은요/는요 is used only in spoken language to ask the other person, typically paired with a noun to emphasize the follow-up question about that noun.\nIn Chinese, "还没" corresponds almost one-to-one with 아직 안/못, but 아직도 carries a surprised tone of "even now...?" and is stronger than 아직.

这节课学两个口语必备小词：\\n아직（还/仍然）常配否定句，아직 안 했어요 =.en:
This lesson covers two essential spoken-language particles:
아직 (still/yet) often pairs with negative sentences, e.g., 아직 안 했어요 = haven't done it yet;
은요/는요 attaches to a noun to ask "what about...?"—the simplest way to follow up with the other person.
Both are extremely frequent in everyday conversation.

아직 放在否定词前：\\n아직 안/못/지 않다。\\n아직도 语气更强，带惊讶.en:
아직 is placed before negative words: 
아직 안/못/지 않다. 
아직도 carries a stronger tone, with surprise or impatience. 
아직 can also be used with positive sentences to mean "still doing": 
아직 공부해요 (still studying). 
The batchim rule for 은요/는요: 
If the noun ends with a batchim (final consonant) → 은요, if not → 는요.

\"你作业交了吗？\"\"还没。\\n\"\"那小明呢？\"아직 和 은요/는요.en:
"Did you submit your homework?" "Not yet.
" "What about Ming?" 아직 and 은요/는요 are the most natural expressions when talking about progress or asking about someone's situation. 
You'll see them everywhere—when binge-watching shows, asking friends about progress, or in classroom interactions. 
Once you learn these two, your conversations will flow much more smoothly.

问别人打算，说做完再做.en: Ask about someone's plans, or say you'll do something after finishing another

-을/ㄹ 건가요? 仅用于疑问句的口语表达，表示对将来打算的询问；\\n-고 나.en:
-을/ㄹ 건가요? is a colloquial expression used only in questions to ask about future intentions; 
-고 나서 means to do the next action only after the previous one is completely finished, emphasizing order and completion. 
The difference between -고 나서 and -고: 
-고 only connects actions in sequence, while -고 나서 emphasizes that "the first thing is truly done." 
In Chinese, "do after finishing" relies on separate words like "再" or "然后," but Korean uses -고 나서 to embed the sense of "completion" directly into the connective ending.

这节课学\"问别人计划\"和\"先做完再做\"：\\n-을/ㄹ 건가요? 是询问.en: In this lesson, you'll learn how to "ask about someone's plans" and say "do something after finishing another": \n-을/ㄹ 건가요? is a colloquial question used to ask about someone's future intentions; \n-고 나서 emphasizes the order and completion of actions, equivalent to "after finishing..."

-을/ㄹ 건가요? 的收音规则与 -을/ㄹ 거예요 相同：\\n有收音→을 건가.en:
The batchim rule for -을/ㄹ 건가요? is the same as -을/ㄹ 거예요: 
With batchim → 을 건가요?, without batchim or with ㄹ → ㄹ 건가요?. 
It is only used in questions, not in statements. 
-고 나서 attaches directly to the verb stem + 고, and 나서 is fixed. 
나서 comes from 나다 (to end/come out), emphasizing the meaning of "completion."

\"你今天下班后打算做什么？\"\"等我吃完饭再出发。\\n\"\"作业做完再玩.en:
"What do you plan to do after work today?" "I'll leave after I finish eating.
" "Finish your homework before playing.
" Asking about plans and describing the order of tasks is fundamental to daily conversation. 
With -을/ㄹ 건가요? and -고 나서, you can smoothly arrange things and discuss plans.

说\"要是……就麻烦了\"，或彻底做完.en: Say "if... it'll be a big problem," or express doing something completely

-(으)면 큰일이다 常用于口语，表示\"要是……的话，就麻烦了\"；\\n-아.en: -(으)면 큰일이다 is commonly used in spoken language to mean "if... then it's a big problem"; \n-아/어/여 버리다 is used in spoken language to indicate that an action or event is completely finished, carrying a nuance of "doing it all at once" or "completely losing/consuming something." \nThe Chinese "完了/糟了" corresponds to 큰일이다, but Korean emphasizes the "hypothetical" with -(으)면 to introduce the worrying situation.

这节课学两种表达强烈情绪的句型：\\n-(으)면 큰일이다 表示\"一旦发生就麻.en: This lesson covers two sentence patterns for expressing strong emotions: \n-(으)면 큰일이다 means "if it happens, it's a big problem/disaster" (worry/warning tone); \n-아/어/여 버리다 attaches to verbs to indicate the action is completely done, sometimes with a light feeling, sometimes with regret, depending on the context.

-(으)면 큰일이다 的收音规则同 -(으)면：\\n有收音→으면 큰일이다，无.en:
The final consonant rule for -(으)면 큰일이다 is the same as -(으)면: 
With a final consonant → 으면 큰일이다, without a final consonant → 면 큰일이다. 
The connection rule for -아/어/여 버리다 is the same as the 해요 form: 
Positive vowels (ㅏ/ㅗ) → 아 버리다, others → 어 버리다, 하다 → 해 버리다. 
버리다 itself can change tense: 
버렸어요 (completely finished).

\"要是错过末班车就麻烦了！\"\"把零食全吃完了\"\"手机电量用完了\"这两.en: "If I miss the last train, it'll be a disaster!" "I ate all the snacks" "My phone battery is completely drained" — these expressions are natural for conveying worry, regret, or a sense of relief upon completion. \n버리다 is often used in everyday conversation and when complaining about shows, adding emotional color to your Korean.

判断对错：-(으)면 큰일이다 和 -아/어 버리다.en: True or False: -(으)면 큰일이다 and -아/어 버리다

用于口语中，表示\"觉得……，认为……\"。\\n动词接 -는/ㄴ다고 생각하다.en:
Used in spoken language to mean "feel that...", "think that...".
Verbs take -는/ㄴ다고 생각하다, adjectives take -다고 생각하다, and nouns take -(이)라고 생각하다.
It can be used as a sentence ending, or followed by a connective ending.
In Chinese, "I think/feel" has only one form, but in Korean, the form changes depending on whether the following word is a verb, adjective, or noun—this is the core challenge of this lesson.

这节课学\"表达观点\"的句型框架。\\n韩语说\"我觉得……\"时，中间那个\.en: This lesson covers the sentence pattern for expressing opinions.\nIn Korean, when saying "I think...", the part in the middle must change form: verbs → -는/ㄴ다고, adjectives → -다고, nouns → -(이)라고, and finally all connect to 생각해요.\nRemember the three entry points, and expressing opinions becomes easy.

动词收音规则：\\n有收音→-는다고（먹는다고），无收音→-ㄴ다고（가다→간다고.en:
Verb final-consonant rules: with a final consonant → -는다고 (먹는다고), without a final consonant → -ㄴ다고 (가다→간다고).
Adjectives directly take -다고 (예쁘다고, 맛있다고).
Nouns: with a final consonant → 이라고, without a final consonant → 라고.
For past tense, uniformly use -았/었다고 생각해요.

\"我觉得那首歌很好听\"\"你觉得这家店怎么样？\"\"我认为他是个好人\"表.en: "I think that song is really good" "What do you think of this store?" "I think he's a good person"—expressing personal opinions is a core skill in all conversations.\nWhen watching variety shows, discussing drama plots, or chatting with Korean friends, -다고 생각해요 is one of the sentence patterns you'll need most.

날 是名词，表示\"日子、那天\"。\\n动词和形容词与 날 相连时需要搭配冠词.en:
날 is a noun meaning "day" or "that day."
When verbs and adjectives connect with 날, they need to use the adnominal form;
nouns directly use (의) 날.
It is used to describe a specific point in time or a day with a particular quality.
This is an extension of the adnominal forms from Chapter 5—you've already learned how -는/은/ㄴ modify nouns. This lesson focuses specifically on using them with 날 to experience the high-frequency scenario of "describing a day."
In Chinese, "the day it rains" directly combines an adjective with a noun, but in Korean, you must choose between -는/-은/-ㄴ depending on whether it's a verb or adjective and whether there's a final consonant—the rules are more complex than in Chinese.

这节课是冠词形的专项练习：\\n动词现在时(-는 날)、动词过去时(-은/ㄴ 날.en: This lesson is a focused practice on adnominal forms:\nThree forms modify 날: verb present tense (-는 날), verb past tense (-은/ㄴ 날), and adjective (-은/ㄴ 날).\nThe core logic is exactly the same as modifying other nouns, but 날 is especially common in everyday conversation, so it's worth practicing separately.

动词现在冠词形：\\n直接词干 + -는（不看收音）。\\n动词过去冠词形：\\.en:
Verb present adnominal form:
Stem + -는 (regardless of final consonant).
Verb past adnominal form:
With final consonant → -은 날, without final consonant or with ㄹ → -ㄴ 날.
Adjective adnominal form:
With final consonant → -은 날, without final consonant → -ㄴ 날 (adjectives also use -은/ㄴ in present tense).
Verbs/adjectives ending in ㄹ:
ㄹ-final verbs → -는 날 (살다→사는 날); adjectives → -ㄴ 날 (길다→긴 날).

\"第一次见面的那天\"\"心情好的日子就出去逛\"\"今天是休息的日子\"描述.en: "The day we first met," "On days when I'm in a good mood, I go out for a walk," "Today is a day of rest"—describing specific days is essential for writing diaries, sharing feelings, and recalling memories.\nKPOP lyrics are full of 날 usage; after this lesson, you'll be able to understand more lyrics.

礼貌确认没听清的内容.en: Politely confirm something you didn't hear clearly

얼마/누구/어디/언제/무엇(뭐) + -(이)라고 하다 表示说话人没听清对方.en: 얼마/누구/어디/언제/무엇(뭐) + -(이)라고 하다 is used when the speaker didn't hear the other person clearly or wants to confirm, equivalent to "What did you say...?" in English.\n사정이 있다 is mainly used in spoken language, meaning "to have a reason, to have circumstances, to have a constraint."\nThe Chinese "来着" corresponds to -(이)라고 했지요?—use a question word to "locate" the part you didn't hear, then add 라고 하다 to express reported confirmation.

这节课学\"没听清时怎么礼貌确认\"。\\n用疑问词（얼마/누구/어디/언제/뭐.en: This lesson covers "how to politely confirm when you didn't hear clearly."\nUse a question word (얼마/누구/어디/언제/뭐) in place of the part you didn't hear, then attach 라고 했지요? or 라고 하셨지요?\n사정이 있다 is a standalone phrase meaning "to have a reason/constraint," often used to politely decline or explain why you're leaving early.

얼마/누구/어디/언제 结尾无收音，直接接 라고 하다。\\n무엇 有收音→이라.en:
얼마/누구/어디/언제 end without a final consonant, so they directly take 라고 하다.
무엇 has a final consonant → 이라고 하다;
The colloquial shortened form 뭐 has no final consonant → 라고 하다 (뭐라고 했지요?).
Politeness levels:
하다→했지요? (standard), 하셨지요? (honorific).
사정이 있다/사정이 생겼다 (there's a reason/something came up) are both commonly used.

\"您说价格是多少来着？\"\"刚才说是谁？\"\"不好意思，我有点事先走了\".en: "What did you say the price was?" "Who did you say it was earlier?" "Sorry, I have something to take care of, so I'll head out first"—these three situations come up when shopping, asking for directions, or leaving a gathering.\n사정이 있다 is the universal polite excuse for leaving, and -라고 했지요? is the standard pattern for confirming information—both are extremely practical.

说\"担心能不能……\"和\"没多久\".en: Saying "worried whether I can..." and "not long since"

-을/ㄹ 수 있을지 걱정이다 是固定句式，用于口语，表示\"担心能不能做某事\.en: -을/ㄹ 수 있을지 걱정이다 is a fixed pattern used in spoken language to mean "worried about whether one can do something";\n-은/ㄴ 지(가) 얼마 안 되다 is a fixed pattern commonly used in spoken language, equivalent to "it hasn't been long since doing..." in Chinese.\nIn Chinese, "worried whether I can..." is said directly, but Korean uses -을지 to "embed" that uncertainty—this is the fixed way Korean expresses indirect worry.

这节课学两个固定句式。\\n第一个：\\n-을/ㄹ 수 있을지 걱정이다，把\".en:
This lesson covers two fixed sentence patterns.
First:
-을/ㄹ 수 있을지 걱정이다, packaging "concern about ability" into one sentence;
Second:
-은/ㄴ 지 얼마 안 되다, using the past adnominal form + 지 to express "not much time has passed since doing that thing."
Both are fixed combinations, so memorizing them as whole units is most efficient.

-을/ㄹ 수 있을지：\\n有收音→을지，无收音/ㄹ→ㄹ지，规则与 -을/ㄹ 수.en:
-을/ㄹ 수 있을지:
With a final consonant → 을지, without a final consonant or with ㄹ → ㄹ지, following the same rules as -을/ㄹ 수 있다.
-은/ㄴ 지 얼마 안 되다:
Verb past adnominal form + 지 (with final consonant → -은 지, without → -ㄴ 지).
Time expressions:
얼마 안 됐어요 (not long ago) / 이제 막 됐어요 (just now).
The 가 in 지(가) can be omitted.

\"担心自己韩语够不够好\"\"来韩国没多久还不熟悉\"\"学韩语没多久\"初学.en: "Worried whether my Korean is good enough," "not familiar yet since I just came to Korea," "haven't been studying Korean long" — super useful for beginners introducing themselves or explaining their level.\nBoth patterns carry a humble, honest tone, which leaves a good impression in Korean culture.

选择正确的担心/经历表达.en: Choose the Correct Expression for Worry/Experience

说\"连想都不敢想\"，也说思念.en: Say "can't even think of it" and express longing
